newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Dostum replaces mutinous general in Afghan north.
newsitem.headline: Dostum replaces mutinous general in Afghan north.

text.p: Northern Afghan opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum on Wednesday replaced a mutinous commander who proclaimed an uprising this week in favour of the purist Islamic Taleban militia, diplomatic sources said.
They said Dostum had appointed Alen Razem, a former air force commander, to replace General Abdul Malik as governor of Faryab province, west of Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Witnesses said Mazar-i-Sharif was generally calm and the Afghan currency, the Afghani, had bounced back to 68,000 to the dollar after touching a low of about 90,000 on Tuesday.
It remains unclear how much territory Dostum has lost to Malik's forces or the Taleban since the mutiny began early on Monday, and there have been few reports of heavy fighting.
U.N. officials said there had been no sign that ordinary people had been displaced by the latest turmoil in the north, but added they were on alert for any such movements.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) service said Malik, in control of Maimana, the capital of Faryab province, had handed over 700 prisoners to the Taleban on Tuesday evening.
It said they were former Dostum fighters or members of Ittehad-i-Islami, a Sunni Moslem guerrilla faction aligned with the former government led by president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
AIP said the Taleban had demanded that Malik also hand over former Herat provincial governor Ismail Khan, who had been fighting the Islamic militia in northwestern Afghanistan.
Khan, a renowned guerrilla commander, was forced to flee to Iran after the Taleban captured Herat in September 1995.
Apart from Malik's seizure of Maimana, where white Taleban flags appeared and Dostum portraits were torn down on Monday, the fate of other northern provinces remains uncertain.

Malik, the brother of Rasul Pahlivan, a Dostum commander who was assassinated in Mazar-i-Sharif last year, has accused Dostum of trying to split Afghanistan. But his apparent pro-Taleban stance has puzzled observers, who see deep differences between the ethnic Uzbeks of the north and the mainly Pashtun Taleban.

Another disaffected Dostum commander, General Majid Rouzi, told the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) on Tuesday that members of Dostum's Junbish-i-Milli faction had decided to dislodge him because he was a "national traitor".
Dostum, who fought for the pro-communist government of the late president Najibullah until 1992, has a history of switching his allegiances at critical moments in Afghanistan.
He went over to the anti-Soviet mujahideen guerrillas in April 1992, enabling them to take over Kabul from Najibullah.
He also staged an unsuccessful revolt, in alliance with former prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, against Rabbani and his military chief, Ahmad Shah Masood, in Kabul in January 1994.
Dostum then linked up with his old rival Masood and the Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat militia to form a loose military alliance after the Taleban captured Kabul in September.

The northern alliance, said by the Taleban to receive support from Iran, Uzbekistan and Russia, is the last force blocking the Taleban's ambition to impose their strict interpretation of Islamic sharia law throughout Afghanistan.
The Taleban have made clear that an amnesty offered to their opponents if they surrender will not apply to Dostum.
When the Taleban seized Kabul, one of their first actions was to hang Najibullah, along with his brother, after seizing him from a U.N. compound where he had been staying.
